clinicalPearls: A congenital cystic dilatation of the biliary tree, most often affecting the extrahepatic common bile duct, and more common in females and in East Asian populations
The classic triad of abdominal pain, jaundice, and a palpable right upper quadrant mass is present in only a minority; most children show one or two of these features
Infants often present with obstructive jaundice and an abdominal mass, whereas older children more often have intermittent pain and cholangitis
The Todani classification describes the anatomical types, with type I (fusiform extrahepatic dilatation) being the most frequent
An anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction allowing reflux of pancreatic enzymes into the bile duct is thought to contribute to many cases
Ultrasound is the usual first-line study, with MRCP providing detailed mapping of the biliary anatomy before surgery
Treatment is complete excision of the cyst with reconstruction by hepaticojejunostomy, because the abnormal epithelium carries a lifelong risk of malignancy
Even after excision, long-term surveillance is needed for anastomotic stricture, recurrent cholangitis, and biliary malignancy
reference.pathophysiology: Choledochal cysts are congenital dilatations of part of the biliary tree. A widely accepted mechanism is an anomalous union of the pancreatic and bile ducts outside the duodenal wall, creating a long common channel that allows pancreatic secretions to reflux into the biliary system. Enzymatic damage weakens and dilates the duct wall, and chronic inflammation predisposes the abnormal biliary epithelium to stricturing, stone formation, cholangitis, and, over time, malignant change (cholangiocarcinoma).
additionalDifferentials: Obstruction from a biliary or gallstone
additionalInvestigations: Abdominal ultrasound as the initial imaging test
Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography to delineate biliary and pancreaticobiliary anatomy
Liver function tests and inflammatory markers to assess cholestasis and cholangitis
Serum amylase/lipase if pancreatitis is suspected
Intraoperative cholangiography when needed to clarify ductal anatomy
redFlags: Ascending cholangitis with fever, pain, and jaundice requiring prompt treatment
Cyst rupture causing biliary peritonitis, a surgical emergency
Features suggesting malignant transformation, especially in longstanding or previously untreated cysts
Progressive obstructive jaundice with signs of biliary sepsis
reference.prognosis: Complete surgical excision with biliary reconstruction gives good long-term results in most children and reduces but does not abolish the malignancy risk. Internal drainage procedures that leave the cyst in place are inadequate because they carry ongoing risks of cholangitis, stones, and cancer, so lifelong follow-up remains important.
pitfalls: Performing simple internal drainage rather than complete cyst excision, leaving malignancy risk
Confusing neonatal presentation with biliary atresia and delaying appropriate imaging
Failing to identify and address an anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction
Neglecting long-term surveillance for late strictures, cholangitis, and biliary cancer
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Definitive treatment is complete surgical excision of the cyst with Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy to restore biliary drainage
Avoid internal drainage or cyst-enterostomy procedures that leave epithelium in situ, as they carry ongoing risk of cholangitis, stones and malignancy
Treat intercurrent cholangitis with broad-spectrum antibiotics and biliary decompression before definitive surgery
Tailor the operation to Todani type, with cyst excision and hepaticojejunostomy for extrahepatic types and endoscopic sphincterotomy for a type III choledochocele
Undertake lifelong surveillance with liver function tests and imaging for anastomotic stricture, intrahepatic stones and residual cholangiocarcinoma risk
Manage within a paediatric surgery and hepatology multidisciplinary team
